t.1.72.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, as he set out for the abode of the thirty gods, having completed his vow and been dismissed by his teacher, Devayānī spoke these words to him.
t.1.72.2: O grandson of the seer Aṅgiras, you shine by your conduct and your noble lineage, by your learning, by your austerity, and by your self-restraint.
t.1.72.3: Just as the illustrious seer Aṅgiras is to be honored by my father, so is Bṛhaspati to be honored and revered all the more by me.
t.1.72.4: Knowing this, understand what I am telling you, O man rich in austerities: how I have conducted myself toward you while you were steadfast in your vows and devoted to your observances.
t.1.72.5: Now that you have completed your learning and returned, you ought to accept me, who am devoted to you. Take my hand in due form, accompanied by the sacred mantras.
t.1.72.6: Just as your father, the blessed lord, is to be worshipped and honored by me, so you, O lady of flawless limbs, are even more worthy of my reverence.
t.1.72.8: Just as Śukra, your father, is my guru and ever worthy of my reverence, so too are you, Devayānī; you should not speak to me thus.
t.1.72.7: You, good lady, are dearer to the great-souled Bhārgava than his own life-breaths; by dharma you, my guru's daughter, are always worthy of honor from me.
t.1.72.9: You are indeed the son of the son of my father's guru, but you are not the son of my father; therefore, best of the twice-born, you are worthy of honor and reverence for me as well.
t.1.72.10: And, Kaca, when you were being slain by the asuras again and again, the love I have borne you from that time on, you yourself should remember it.
t.1.72.11: You know my supreme devotion, in friendship and in affection; O knower of dharma, you ought not to abandon me, devoted and blameless as I am.
t.1.72.12: You urge upon me a task that ought never to be urged, O you of auspicious vows. Be gracious to me, fair-browed one; to me you are more venerable even than my guru, O lovely one.
t.1.72.14: By dharma you are my sister; do not speak thus, O fair-faced one. I have dwelt here happily, good lady, and I bear no anger.
t.1.72.13: Where you once dwelt, wide-eyed, moon-faced one, there I too have dwelt, good lady, in the belly of Kāvya, O spirited one.
t.1.72.17: It is because I regard you as my guru's daughter that I refuse you, not because of any fault in you; and I have been given leave by my guru. Curse me, then, as you please.
t.1.72.19: Therefore the desire that you cherish shall not come to pass as you wish; no son of a seer shall ever take your hand in marriage.
t.1.72.18: O Devayānī, I was speaking the law of the seers, yet I have been cursed by you, though I do not deserve the curse. You have done it today out of desire, not out of dharma.
t.1.72.21: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to Devayānī, Kaca, the best of the twice-born, that most excellent of Brahmins, then went swiftly to the abode of the lord of the thirty gods.
t.1.72.23: Since you have performed a most wondrous deed for our benefit, your fame shall never perish, and you shall have a share with us.
t.1.72.22: Seeing him arrive, the gods led by Indra honored Bṛhaspati and, filled with joy, spoke these words to Kaca.
t.1.72.20: What you told me, that my knowledge will not bear fruit, let it be so; but the one whom I shall teach, his knowledge will bear fruit.
t.1.72.15: I take leave of you and shall go; wish me well upon my way. Without offense to dharma, I am to be remembered in the course of your conversation. Always vigilant and ready, serve my teacher faithfully.
t.1.72.16: If, when urged by me for the sake of dharma and love, you reject me, then, Kaca, this knowledge of yours will not attain success.
